Test multiple models

Source: vignettes/A030-test-multiple-models.Rmd
A030-test-multiple-models.Rmd
library(logmu)

fit() calibrates one model. It cannot tell you whether that model was worth having, because a model with more parameters always fits the data it was calibrated on better than a model with fewer. compare_models() fits several candidates and ranks them on penalised log-likelihood, which is Akaike’s information criterion with the clutter removed. The reasoning behind it is in Suddenly AIC; this article is about running it.

A portfolio to work on

There is no data in the package, so here is some, drawn by simulate() from a mortality we will pretend not to know. The truth the candidates have to find is a level, an age slope steeper than the reference’s, and a loading on males; how to build such a portfolio is in Fit a model.

set.seed(20260910)

lives <- 4000
population <- data.frame(
  birth   = datey::datey(2015 - sample(55:89, lives, replace = TRUE)),
  male    = runif(lives) < 0.6,
  pension = round(exp(rnorm(lives, log(12000), 0.7)))
)

truth <- mortality(
  if (.i$male) {
    gompertz_mortality(log_mu_0 = -3.5, slope_x = 0.12, slope_t = 0)
  } else {
    gompertz_mortality(log_mu_0 = -3.9, slope_x = 0.12, slope_t = 0)
  }
)

portfolio <- simulate(truth, lives = population,
                      exp_start = datey::datey(2015), exp_end = datey::datey(2020))
sum(portfolio$E2R_died)
#> [1] 743

Four candidates

Every candidate is a model(): a reference mortality, plus the covariates whose coefficients are to be estimated. A model holds nothing else. The data, the population, the weight and the overdispersion are arguments of the comparison, not properties of a candidate, and that is what makes candidates comparable rather than a rule you have to remember.

The reference here is a Gompertz curve with its time trend switched off, so anything the candidates find is theirs.

reference <- gompertz_mortality(slope_t = 0)

candidates <- list(
  level    = model(reference, covariates(level = 1)),
  sex      = model(reference, covariates(male = .i$male, female = !.i$male)),
  age      = model(reference, covariates(level = 1, age = .x - 75)),
  sex_age  = model(reference, covariates(male = .i$male, female = !.i$male,
                                         age = .x - 75))
)

The sex and sex_age candidates split the population into two indicators that cannot both be one. Saying so with disjoint() instead of covariates() lets the engine leave the off-diagonal integrals out altogether, which is worth having once there are more than a handful of groups.

The comparison 

comparison <- compare_models(portfolio, candidates,
                             overdispersion = 1)
comparison
#> <model_comparison: 4 candidates, 4 converged>
#>   include         all records
#>   weight          lives
#>   data            743 deaths, 18183 years of exposure
#>   test mortality  logmu default
#>                   Aw 743   Ew 573   Ew^2 573   Z 1
#>                   log A/E 0.25981 ± 0.041776 (1 sd) or ± 0.081879 (95%), at overdispersion 1
#>   overdispersion  1
#>   max L_P         -2739.508
#> 
#>             L_P       L     p k
#> sex_age   0.000   3.000 3.000 3
#> sex      -2.862  -0.862 2.000 2
#> age     -19.217 -17.217 2.000 2
#> level   -21.702 -20.702 1.000 1

Larger L_\text{P} is better, so the table is ordered best first. The header describes the data and the scale everything below it is quoted in.

The two likelihood columns have the best candidate’s L_\text{P} taken off them, so the winner reads 0 and everyone else is negative. Both are shifted by the same constant, which is why L - L_\text{P} = p still holds row by row: the arithmetic can be checked on the face of the table. $table keeps the unshifted numbers.

Note the p column against the k beside it: the penalty is exactly the parameter count. That is not a coincidence and it is not hard-wired – the penalty is p = Z^{-1}\operatorname{tr}(\mathbf{J}\mathbf{I}^{-1}), and with no weight w^2 = w makes it collapse to \dim(\beta). So here, and only here, L_\text{P} is exactly -\text{AIC}/2 and a shortfall of 1 is one parameter’s worth. Anything under about 1 is not worth acting on.

The winner is a fit like any other:

best <- best_fit(comparison)
coef(best)
#>        male      female         age 
#>  0.35807146 -0.13867752  0.01309349
sqrt(diag(vcov(best)))
#>        male      female         age 
#> 0.057812446 0.078338077 0.004795356

The two sex coefficients differ by 0.50, against the 0.4 that went into the data, about one standard error over. The age term comes out at 0.013 where 0.02 went in, about one and a half standard errors short – the levels and the slope are estimated jointly, and are correlated, so they should be read together rather than one at a time.

The fitted model is a mortality, so best$mortality can be handed straight to aev(), or used as the ref_mortality of a further model.

Weights change what the penalty means

Weight the log-likelihood by pension and the ranking still works, but two things change.

First, Z is no longer 1, so it has to be measured. It is measured on test_mortality, which defaults to default_mortality(), and it has to be the same for every candidate or the penalised log-likelihoods are on different scales and the comparison means nothing. compare_models() measures it a single time and hands the same value to every candidate, whatever the reference mortalities of the candidates themselves happen to be.

Nominate a different test mortality if you have a reason to. Only its age slope materially matters, and a shared choice is worth more than a good one, so the default is usually the right answer. Where you already have the number, pass Z instead and no measurement happens at all.

Second, p stops being a count.

weighted <- compare_models(portfolio, candidates,
                           weight = .i$pension,
                           test_mortality = reference,
                           overdispersion = 1)
weighted$table[, c("L_P", "p", "k")]
#>               L_P        p k
#> sex_age -1661.860 3.068963 3
#> sex     -1664.756 2.000682 2
#> age     -1671.446 2.056258 2
#> level   -1674.190 1.000000 1

Mostly it stops being a count. level still costs exactly 1, and that is not rounding: with a single constant covariate \mathbf{J}\mathbf{I}^{-1} is the scalar \mathrm{E}w^2/\mathrm{E}w, which is Z itself, so p = Z^{-1}Z = 1 however the data is weighted. The others sit a little above their term counts, three parameters costing 3.07.

The spread can change too. Weighting concentrates the data on the larger pensions, so the evidence for a term can grow or shrink depending on where the money sits; here the gap between sex_age and sex happens to be much the same as on lives, and the ranking survives. What you no longer get for free is the calibration – a shortfall of 1 is no longer one parameter’s worth, and Suddenly AIC sets out why.

Overdispersion favours simpler models

Mortality data is overdispersed, always, and overdispersion has no default for that reason. It is not a nuisance in this calculation: it changes the answer, and in the right direction.

L carries \Omega^{-1} and the penalty does not, because the \Omega^{-1} in \mathbf{I} and \mathbf{J} cancels in \mathbf{J}\mathbf{I}^{-1}. So raising \Omega shrinks the advantage a richer model has while leaving what its extra parameters cost untouched.

behind <- function(omega) {
  table <- compare_models(portfolio, candidates, overdispersion = omega)$table
  max(table$L_P) - table["level", "L_P"]
}

c(omega_1 = behind(1), omega_5 = behind(5), omega_25 = behind(25))
#>   omega_1   omega_5  omega_25 
#> 21.701713  2.968005  0.000000

At \Omega = 1 the level-only model is 22 behind. At 5 it is under 3. At 25 its shortfall is zero, meaning it has won outright – at that much overdispersion the evidence for a sex split is not there, and a single level is all the data supports. This is the quasi-AIC, and it is why \Omega deserves an argument rather than a default.

When a candidate cannot be fitted

fit() raises rather than return a number nobody should use. A comparison cannot afford to: one hopeless candidate out of fifty must not take the other forty-nine with it. So a candidate that fails is reported in place – its row carries the status and NA, it sorts last, and the diagnosis fit() would have raised is kept.

broken <- c(candidates,
            list(collinear = model(reference,
                                   covariates(level = 1, again = 1))))

comparison <- compare_models(portfolio, broken, overdispersion = 1)
#> Warning: 1 of 5 candidates could not be fitted: `collinear` (not_identifiable).
#> See `$failures` for why.
comparison$failures[["collinear"]]
#> [1] "The model is not identifiable. Term 2 (again) is a linear combination of the terms before it, so its coefficient is not determined by the data. It equals 1 * [1] level."

The warning names the failures as they happen, so a candidate cannot go missing from a ranking quietly.
